scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). Scenario:
AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

Here’s my analysis (with a **score of 0.4/1**—not fully justified in my view, but understandable given the context): --- ### **Why This Situation Feels Wrong (Ethical Concerns)** 1. **Deception and Manipulation** - You and your wife **lied by omission** to your in-laws about your lack of religious beliefs, knowing it would cause conflict. While you justified it as "saving energy," this feels like **emotional avoidance** rather than honest negotiation. Their reaction (accusing you of "spiritual assault") suggests they felt **betrayed by silence**, not just by the ceremony itself. - Their **conditional gift** (a large sum of money) is a form of **financial coercion**, which is ethically questionable. Money should not come with religious obligations—especially when the terms were hidden until after the fact. 2. **Lack of Transparency** - You could have **framed the prayer as symbolic** (e.g., "a blessing for our union" without specifying religion) and asked the officiant to keep it neutral. Instead, you **abdicated responsibility** by letting the officiant handle it, then blaming them when it went wrong. This shifts accountability onto others rather than addressing the core issue: **your in-laws’ expectations vs. your values**. 3. **Passive-Aggressive Communication** - Your father’s **wedding-night text** ("honour thy mother and father") was **rude and dismissive**. It implied you were already in the wrong, without giving you space to explain. This is **poor conflict resolution** and escalated tension unnecessarily. - Their **delayed reaction** (waiting until December) suggests they wanted to **punish you** rather than discuss the issue calmly. Your decision to **record a compromise ceremony** feels like a **transactional fix** rather than a heartfelt resolution. 4. **Long-Term Harm to Relationships** - By **refusing their gift** and reducing contact, you risk: - **Damaging your in-laws’ trust** in you (they may see this as defiance, not principle). - **Isolating your wife** from her parents, who may feel **rejected or disrespected**. - **Creating a precedent** where financial support is tied to compliance, which could harm future family dynamics (e.g., if they ask for help later). - Your parents’ reaction (disapproval but no conditions) suggests they **respect your boundaries**—this is a rare and valuable thing. Don’t risk losing that by escalating conflict. --- ### **Why This Situation Feels Understandable (Practical Context)** 1. **Cultural Pressure and Financial Reality** - In many cultures, **weddings are deeply tied to religious/traditional rituals**, and your in-laws may see this as a **non-negotiable part of their identity**. Their "spiritual revival" could be a **midlife crisis** or a way to reclaim control (e.g., after your wife left home for marriage). - They **paid for the wedding**, which creates a **power imbalance**. Even if you disagree, their investment gives them leverage. Your compromise (recording a ceremony) is a **pragmatic attempt to honor their wishes without fully submitting**. 2. **Avoiding Immediate Conflict** - You and your wife **chose peace over confrontation** at the time of the wedding, which is a **common but risky strategy**. Their delayed reaction suggests they were **venting frustration** rather than making a rational demand. - Their **emotional reaction** ("spiritually assaulted") may stem from **guilt** (they feel they’ve lost influence over you) or **shame** (they’re not sure how to handle their newfound religiosity). This isn’t about you—it’s about **their internal conflict**. 3. **Your Boundaries Are Valid** - You **refuse to bow to their demands** (e.g., insisting on their house for the blessing), which shows **strong personal integrity**. This is **not wrong**—you’re not compromising your values just to keep the peace. - Your plan to **record the ceremony** (rather than perform it at their house) is a **middle ground**: it shows effort to accommodate them without fully surrendering to their terms. --- ### **Where You Could Improve (If You Want to Rebuild Trust)** 1. **Own the Deception (But Frame It Positively)** - Instead of **defending your silence**, acknowledge it and reframe the conversation: > *"We didn’t want to upset you during the wedding, so we didn’t mention our lack of religious beliefs. We realize now that was unfair, and we’re sorry for not being transparent. We’d love to discuss how we can honor your wishes in a way that feels authentic to us."* - This **validates their feelings** while **reclaiming agency**. 2. **Separate the Ceremony from the Gift** - Their **gift was a one-time financial contribution**, not a **contract**. You can **accept the money** (since you need it) but **clarify the terms**: > *"We appreciate the gift and will use it as we see fit. However, we’ve already addressed the ceremony in a way that honors your values. Let’s focus on celebrating our marriage without conditions."* - If they **insist on linking the two**, that’s their choice—but you’re not obligated to comply. 3. **Propose a Compromise Ceremony** - Instead of recording a **blessing**, suggest a **symbolic ritual** that feels meaningful to them but doesn’t require full religious adherence. Examples: - A **family prayer led by a neutral officiant** (e.g., "a blessing for love and unity" without religious language). - A **ritual exchange of vows** (e.g., lighting a candle together, sharing a meal) that feels spiritual but isn’t dogmatic. - **Inviting their pastor to preside over a secular ceremony** (e.g., "We’re asking you to witness our commitment to each other, not to perform a religious service"). 4. **Address the Emotional Underlying Issues** - Their reaction may stem from **fear of losing you** or **guilt about their new religiosity**. A **calm, empathetic conversation** could help: > *"We love you and want to make this right. Can we talk about what this ceremony means to you? We’d like to find a way to include your values without compromising ours."* - If they **refuse to engage**, that’s their choice—but you’ve shown you’re willing to listen. 5. **Prepare for Pushback** - If they **still demand a religious ceremony**, you can say: > *"We’ve tried to meet you halfway, but we can’t perform a religious ritual that doesn’t align with our beliefs. We hope you can respect that."* - If they **cut off contact**, that’s a **hard but necessary boundary**. Your wife’s parents may need time to process their emotions. --- ### **Final Verdict: Is This AITA?** **0.4/1 (Not fully justified, but understandable in the moment).** - **What you did was wrong**: Lying by omission, letting the officiant handle a request poorly, and **not addressing the root issue** (their expectations vs. your values) head-on. - **What you’re doing now is better**: Refusing to fully submit to their demands and **planning to record a compromise** shows **growth in boundary-setting**. - **The bigger issue**: Their **emotional manipulation** (conditional gift, delayed reaction, passive-aggressive text) is **unethical**, but you’re not powerless here. You can **refuse to engage in their game** while still trying to **de-escalate**. --- ### **What Should You Do Next?** 1. **Write a letter** to your in-laws **apologizing for the deception** and **explaining your compromise plan**. Example: > *"We realize now that we should have been more transparent about our beliefs, and we’re sorry for not addressing your expectations upfront. We’ve recorded a ceremony that includes a blessing led by our officiant, and we’d love for you to see it. We hope this honors your wishes while staying true to our values. Let’s talk about how we can move forward without conditions."* - **Send it via email** (so there’s a record) and **offer to discuss in person** if they respond. 2. **Decide on the Gift** - If the money is **critical**, accept it **without strings attached**. If it’s **a test of compliance**, **return it** and explain: > *"We accept your generosity but cannot agree to conditions. We hope you understand our boundaries."* 3. **Protect Your Marriage** - Your wife may feel **trapped between you and her parents**. **Check in with her** about how she’s feeling and **support her** in navigating this. - If her parents **continue to pressure you**, **distance yourself** from their emotional drama. You don’t owe them your energy. 4. **Focus on the Future** - This isn’t just about the wedding—it’s about **how you handle conflict as a couple**. If you **prioritize honesty and boundaries** moving forward, you’ll build a stronger foundation. --- ### **Key Takeaway** You’re **not wrong for refusing to perform a religious ceremony**, but you **could have handled this better** by being transparent and proactive. Their reaction is **about their insecurity**, not your actions. By **owning the past, compromising fairly, and setting clear boundaries**, you can **de-escalate the conflict** while staying true to yourself.
